lesson.subtitle: Lesson 21 -- When the Attending Asks
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Diego Leonel George Wached | Lesson 21 -- When the Attending Asks

listenings.text: Every month our department holds a meeting called the M and M, morbidity and mortality. Residents present a case that went wrong, or almost went wrong, and we talk about it without blame. The first rule is simple: we never ask who made the mistake. We ask what we could have done differently. So the language of the meeting is the language of the past that did not happen. If we had double-checked the dose, the patient would not have had the reaction. If the handoff had been complete, the night team would have seen the red flag. Notice the form: had plus the past participle in the if part, and would have in the result. And sometimes the result is still with us today. If we had biopsied that lesion in March, the patient would not need a big surgery now. That is the most important part of any debrief: what we learn, and what we will do next time.

My worst week as a resident started with a small oversight. I prescribed an antibiotic for a skin infection, and I did not read the patient's old chart. The allergy was there, on the second page. Two hours later, the pharmacist called me. She said: doctor, this patient is allergic to this drug. Are you sure? I was not sure at all. If she had not called me, the patient would have taken the first dose that night. If I had read the old chart, I would not have made the mistake. It was a near miss, and nobody was hurt. The next morning, I told my attending everything. I took responsibility, and she thanked me for being honest. Today I double-check every allergy before I write a prescription. And to be honest, I would not be the careful doctor I am now if that week had not happened.
